assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks (magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms, proposed by Katori) have pushed frequency measurement to fractional uncertainties around 1e-18, a textbook case of progress being limited by how precisely one can measure. They enable tests of relativity at the cm height scale, searches for varying constants and dark matter, chronometric geodesy and a coming redefinition of the second. From an experimentalist's view the concept is clear, the demonstrations are quantitative and many groups now reproduce and surpass them.
assessment.attribution: Katori made the decisive proposal and early demonstrations of the magic-wavelength lattice clock; Jun Ye's group (Sr clocks, ultra-stable lasers, many-body clock physics) drove the performance to the current record levels. A two-person prize is natural and clean. Others (e.g. Takamoto, Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley) made major contributions but the credited pair is defensible.
assessment.maturity: Highly mature: multiple independent labs (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, SYRTE, PTB, NIST, others) have confirmed and improved the performance over two decades, and the interpretation is stable. Timing is good; the 2005 prize for the frequency comb did not cover the lattice clock concept itself.
uncertainties: How the committee weighs the overlap with the 2005 prize (Hall, Hänsch) and the credit shared with other clock groups.

Whether the redefinition of the second, not yet carried out, would be seen as a prerequisite for recognition. I am relying on my own recollection of the 1e-18 performance figures and have not verified them here.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Matter-wave interferometry with atoms is a new class of precision instrument: gravimeters, gradiometers, measurements of G and of the fine-structure constant, tests of the equivalence principle and prospects for gravitational-wave detection. It fits the principle that new measurement techniques open new ways of observing nature, and quantum sensors for geophysics are now being fielded.
assessment.attribution: Pritchard pioneered atom optics and the first atom interferometers with gratings; Kasevich (with Chu in the 1991 work) demonstrated light-pulse gravimetry and gyroscopes at high sensitivity; Bordé gave the theoretical framework for light-pulse interferometry and the Ramsey-Bordé geometry. Steven Chu, a central figure in light-pulse atom interferometry, is not among the credited names, which weakens the configuration. Chu and Cohen-Tannoudji were already honored in 1997 for cooling, but credit for interferometry remains partly entangled.
assessment.maturity: Mature technique with several independent groups and commercial devices, although headline applications (fundamental tests, gravitational-wave detection) are still developing. Recognition would be timely but not urgent.
uncertainties: Credit allocation between Pritchard, Kasevich, Bordé, Chu and others is not clean.
Whether practical field impact, as opposed to demonstrated sensitivity, is judged sufficient.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED turned superconducting circuits into controllable artificial atoms strongly coupled to single microwave photons, supplying the dispersive readout, gates and architecture that today's superconducting quantum processors rely on. The impact on quantum technology and on quantum optics in a solid-state setting is large and the strong-coupling experiments are clean quantitative demonstrations.
assessment.attribution: The theoretical proposal (Blais, Huang, Wallraff, Girvin, Schoelkopf, 2004) and the first strong-coupling experiment (Wallraff et al., 2004) came from overlapping teams. Girvin is a co-author on the key theory and is left out of my three, so the choice among Girvin, Blais, Schoelkopf and Wallraff is genuinely unsettled. I choose the experimentally decisive pair plus the theoretical proposer.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed across many labs and now industrial platforms. A 2025 prize related to superconducting circuits (macroscopic quantum tunnelling) may make the committee cautious about too close a follow-up, but circuit QED is a different discovery. I recall the 2025 award from memory and have not rechecked it.
uncertainties: Proximity to the recent superconducting-circuits prize and whether it is seen as too similar.
Which of four credited names carries the decisive credit.
Whether the prize should wait for demonstration of useful error-corrected computation.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Cirac-Zoller proposal gave the first concrete scheme for a quantum computer with trapped ions, and Blatt's group demonstrated gates, entanglement and algorithms with exceptional experimental control. Trapped-ion systems remain the benchmark for gate fidelity and coherence. The impact on quantum information is large and the physics is cleanly demonstrated.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller proposed the scheme (1995) and Blatt is one of several leading experimentalists; Wineland (2012 prize) and the NIST group demonstrated the first ion gate, and Monroe and others also deserve credit. The credited triplet pairs theory with a major experimental group but leaves open the question of overlap with Wineland's earlier recognition and with Monroe.
assessment.maturity: Mature, with multiple independent confirming groups and commercial systems. The prior 2012 prize for controlling single quantum systems makes the incremental recognition question important.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2012 Haroche-Wineland prize and with Monroe, Wineland and Kielpinski contributions.
The same theory pair appears in several candidate entries (optical lattices, Rydberg arrays), so the split of their credit across discoveries is unresolved.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical detection and coherent control of single nitrogen-vacancy centres at room temperature created a robust solid-state spin sensor with nanoscale magnetometry, thermometry and bio-sensing applications, and a platform for quantum networks. As an experimentalist I value the strong link between coherence-time engineering and measurement capability, and the breadth of application beyond physics.
assessment.attribution: Wrachtrup and Jelezko made the first single-NV optical detection and control (1997 and subsequent work); Lukin's group extended to nanoscale sensing and quantum registers, though other groups (Awschalom, Hanson, Yacoby, Walsworth, Maze/Hollenberg) were also decisive. Attribution is crowded.
assessment.maturity: Reasonably mature in the basic discovery, with many independent confirmations; the applications and sensing sensitivity are still evolving and many of the technology claims are not yet standard instruments.
uncertainties: Credit is spread across many groups, which makes a three-person selection contentious.
Practical sensitivity advantages over conventional magnetometers remain context-dependent.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices, including the Mott insulator transition and single-site-resolved quantum gas microscopes, provide programmable analog simulators of Hubbard-type models and a way to observe many-body physics with unprecedented control. This opens new ways of observing nature and is a core achievement of modern AMO physics.
assessment.attribution: Bloch and Greiner carried out the key experiments (Mott insulator, microscope), Zoller's proposal with Jaksch, Bruder, Cirac, Gardiner supplied the theoretical foundation, and Dalibard and Cirac are further credited. A three-person subset leaves out important contributors; Jaksch is not among the names.
assessment.maturity: Mature in methodology and widely reproduced; the scientific payoff of quantum simulation in solving open problems is still developing, and some committee members may feel recognition should wait for a decisive new result.
uncertainties: Whether the scientific output so far justifies recognition, versus the instrument-level achievement.
Overlap with the 2001 and 2012 AMO prizes and the other candidate entries sharing Zoller and Cirac.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum key distribution (BB84 and E91) is a conceptually clean application of quantum mechanics to information security, with well-known experimental implementations over fibre and satellite links. It has fundamental importance in linking Bell nonlocality to cryptography. Its practical deployment remains limited, and as an experimentalist I would be cautious about security loopholes in real devices.
assessment.attribution: Bennett and Brassard proposed BB84 and Ekert the entanglement-based protocol; this triplet is a widely discussed configuration, with Wiesner's conjugate coding as a historical precursor not available in the credited names.
assessment.maturity: The concept is old and thoroughly confirmed experimentally, so the recognition is timely if anything late, though the practical significance relative to post-quantum cryptography is debated.
uncertainties: Practical impact versus hype, given post-quantum cryptography.
Wiesner's earlier idea and the role of Bell-inequality-based tests (the 2022 prize) in the credit story.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The quantum cascade laser, based on intersubband transitions in engineered semiconductor heterostructures, created a new class of mid-infrared and terahertz sources used in trace-gas spectroscopy, which is directly relevant to laser spectroscopy and measurement. It is a clear invention with demonstrated device performance, and the first working device (1994) opened a whole field of applications.
assessment.attribution: The 1994 demonstration came from the Bell Labs team led by Capasso, with Faist as lead author and Cho providing molecular-beam epitaxy growth; others (Sirtori, Hutchinson, Kazarinov-Suris for the 1971 proposal) have claims. Kazarinov and Suris are not among the credited names, and the invention-versus-device question will need discussion.
assessment.maturity: Mature: room-temperature continuous-wave operation, commercial products and wide independent adoption. Recognition would be in line with the committee's tradition for laser and semiconductor-device inventions.
uncertainties: Whether the prize belongs to the 1971 theoretical proposal or to the 1994 realization.
Whether this is judged to be engineering rather than a new physical discovery.
